vignette: Ethan is a 21-year-old bus driver who has been struggling with the aftermath of his brief yet intense military service. Ethan enlisted straight out of high school, motivated by a sense of duty and a desire to serve his country. Just five months into his deployment in Afghanistan, he was involved in an IED attack that injured several members of his unit. The event marked a profound shift in Ethan’s life. Every morning when Ethan wakes up, the memory of that day is like a shadow looming over him. He recalls the deafening explosion and the chaos that followed—the smell of smoke, the sound of sirens, and the sight of friends injured or worse. These memories are so vivid that he often wakes from nightmares drenched in sweat, his heart racing as if he were still in harm's way. Driving a bus has been both a lifeline and a challenge for Ethan since his return. The routine of navigating busy streets and interacting with passengers is grounding, but it also brings back unsettling feelings. Sometimes the sound of a car’s horn or a loud noise can trigger a flashback, making him feel like he's right back in that moment when the IED detonated. He will freeze for a few seconds, his hands tightening on the wheel as he tries to regain control. Ethan has become increasingly isolated since returning from deployment. His friends don't seem to understand what he’s been through, and conversations often end with him feeling like an outsider—like no one can truly grasp what it was like to be in that situation. This isolation is compounded by his reluctance to talk about the traumatic event. He avoids discussing military experiences altogether, even with his family, because he fears their reactions might further distance them from each other. Despite these challenges, Ethan still finds moments of normalcy and stability in his job. The bus route has become a familiar path that offers some comfort. Yet, there are days when the trauma feels all too close. He sometimes experiences intense anxiety while driving through crowded areas, imagining potential threats lurking around every corner. This hyper-vigilance makes it difficult to relax even during brief moments of downtime. Ethan’s relationship with his girlfriend has also been affected by these changes. She is supportive and caring but struggles to connect with him emotionally due to his withdrawal. He often cancels plans at the last minute, citing feeling unwell or simply not being in the mood. These cancellations have left her confused and hurt, unsure of how best to support him. Ethan’s attempts to cope include drinking more than he used to, especially on weekends. Alcohol provides a temporary escape from his intrusive thoughts but leaves him feeling even more depleted and disconnected when it wears off. He recognizes that this pattern is not sustainable, yet he finds himself repeating the cycle week after week. In moments of reflection, Ethan wonders if he will ever feel truly at peace again. The bus route has become both a source of comfort and a daily reminder of his struggle to navigate life post-military service. His focus remains on making it through each day as best as he can, hoping that someday the nightmares won't be so vivid, and the anxiety won’t grip him so tightly. Ethan’s story is one of resilience in the face of overwhelming trauma. He continues to find strength in his daily routine while grappling with the lingering shadows of war that have followed him home.
